claim: Extraintestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli (ExPEC) are the leading causes of bacteremia in humans.
source: Extraintestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli (ExPEC), a set of pathogenic E. coli isolates that cause disease outside of the intestine, are the leading causes of bacteremia in humans (Dale and Woodford, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dale and Woodford, 2015

claim: ExPEC strains exhibit markedly delayed clearance from the liver and spleen compared to commensal E. coli in mouse models of systemic infection.
source: In mouse models of systemic infection, ExPEC strains exhibit markedly delayed clearance from the liver and spleen compared to commensal E. coli, suggesting that despite their eventual clearance, ExPEC possess strategies to persist longer within organs, thereby delaying the resolution of infection (Smith et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2010

claim: Replication of Streptococcus pneumoniae within CD169+ splenic macrophages enables systemic dissemination.
source: For example, replication of Streptococcus pneumoniae within CD169+ splenic macrophages (Ercoli et al., 2018) or Staphylococcus aureus within GATA6+ peritoneal macrophages (Jorch et al., 2019) have been shown to enable systemic dissemination.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ercoli et al., 2018

claim: Replication of Staphylococcus aureus within GATA6+ peritoneal macrophages enables systemic dissemination.
source: For example, replication of Streptococcus pneumoniae within CD169+ splenic macrophages (Ercoli et al., 2018) or Staphylococcus aureus within GATA6+ peritoneal macrophages (Jorch et al., 2019) have been shown to enable systemic dissemination.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jorch et al., 2019

claim: STAMP leverages deep sequencing of bacteria barcoded with random DNA sequence tags and population genetics frameworks to quantify bottlenecks, dissemination patterns, and replication rates.
source: One approach known as STAMP (Sequence Tag-Based Analysis of Microbial Populations) leverages deep sequencing of bacteria barcoded with random DNA sequence tags and population genetics frameworks to quantify bottlenecks, dissemination patterns, and, more recently, replication rates (Abel et al., 2015a; Mahmutovic et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abel et al., 2015a and Mahmutovic et al., 2021

claim: STAMP was initially developed to study Vibrio cholerae intestinal colonization.
source: STAMP was initially developed to study Vibrio cholerae intestinal colonization, and subsequently applied to Listeria monocytogenes dissemination from the intestine, P. aeruginosa bacteremia, and S. pneumoniae nasopharyngeal colonization (Bachta et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: STAMPR is a successor to STAMP that relies on a new computational framework and employs additional metrics to study infection population dynamics at higher resolution.
source: We recently created STAMPR, a successor to STAMP that relies on a new computational framework and employs additional metrics to study infection population dynamics at higher resolution (Hullahalli et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hullahalli et al., 2021

claim: Approximately 1100 barcodes were used across over 400 samples from 6 time points and 12 within-animal compartments to map ExPEC population dynamics.
source: Here, we leveraged STAMPR to comprehensively map ExPEC population dynamics following dissemination in blood after intravenous (i.v.) inoculation using ~1100 barcodes across over 400 samples from 6 time points and 12 within-animal compartments.
evidence: Describes the experimental design of the study

claim: ExPEC is largely cleared by most organs, but some organs, most notably the liver, stochastically fail to clear the pathogen.
source: Although ExPEC is largely cleared by most organs, some organs, most notably the liver, stochastically fail to clear the pathogen.
evidence: Summarizes findings from the study

claim: Clearance failures are attributable to the massive expansion of very few bacterial cells from the inoculum.
source: We show that these failures are attributable to the massive expansion of very few bacterial cells from the inoculum and explain the marked variation in bacterial burden observed between animals and organs.
evidence: Describes findings from the study

claim: Clonal expansion underlies the variability in bacterial burden between animals.
source: Clonal expansion underlies the variability in bacterial burden between animals, and stochastic dissemination of clones profoundly alters the pathogen population structure within organs.
evidence: Describes findings from the study

claim: Host bottlenecks are consistent yet highly sensitive to infection variables, including inoculum size and macrophage depletion.
source: Despite variable pathogen expansion events, host bottlenecks are consistent yet highly sensitive to infection variables, including inoculum size and macrophage depletion.
evidence: Describes findings from the study

claim: Bacterial hexose metabolism and cell envelope homeostasis pathways are important for organ-specific pathogen survival.
source: We adapted our barcoding methodology to facilitate multiplexed validation of bacterial fitness determinants identified with transposon mutagenesis and confirmed the importance of bacterial hexose metabolism and cell envelope homeostasis pathways for organ-specific pathogen survival.
evidence: Describes findings from the study

claim: Founding population size (FP) quantifies the number of unique cells from the inoculum that give rise to the pathogen population at a sampling point.
source: FP quantifies the number of unique cells from the inoculum that give rise to the pathogen population at a sampling point.
evidence: Defines a metric used in the study

claim: Higher FP values are indicative of wider (more permissive) bottlenecks.
source: Higher FP values are indicative of wider (more permissive) bottlenecks.
evidence: Explains interpretation of FP metric

claim: FP can be measured by an equation derived by Krimbas and Tsakas, 1971, the output of which is referred to as Nb.
source: FP can be measured by an equation derived by Krimbas and Tsakas, 1971, the output of which is referred to as Nb.
evidence: Supported by citation to Krimbas and Tsakas, 1971

claim: In STAMPR, an algorithmic adjustment is made to Nb that limits the influence of disproportionately abundant barcodes, resulting in a new metric called Nr.
source: In STAMPR, an algorithmic adjustment is made to Nb that limits the influence of disproportionately abundant barcodes, resulting in a new metric called Nr (Hullahalli et al., 2021, mSystems).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hullahalli et al., 2021

claim: The Nr/Nb ratio provides a measure of uniformity of barcode frequencies and is larger in samples where a few bacterial clones have markedly expanded.
source: The degree to which Nb is biased by these 'outliers' can be exploited by calculation of the Nr/Nb ratio, providing a measure of uniformity of barcode frequencies; this ratio is larger in samples where a few bacterial clones have markedly expanded.
evidence: Explains interpretation of Nr/Nb ratio

claim: Approximately 1150 20 nt random and unique sequence barcodes were introduced into the ExPEC strain CFT073 (rpoS+) lacZ locus.
source: We introduced ~1150 20 nt random and unique sequence barcodes into the ExPEC strain CFT073 (rpoS+) (Welch et al., 2002; Ristow and Welch, 2016; Hryckowian and Welch, 2013) lacZ locus.
evidence: Describes experimental methods

claim: The barcodes were stably maintained in the absence of selection for at least ~50 generations.
source: The barcodes were stably maintained in the absence of selection for at least ~50 generations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: The barcodes did not modify the growth rate of the strains in lysogeny broth (LB) media compared to the parental strain.
source: The barcodes were stably maintained in the absence of selection for at least ~50 generations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and did not modify the growth rate of the strains in lysogeny broth (LB) media compared to the parental strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Nr and Nb both accurately quantified in vitro bottlenecks up to 105 CFU for this library.
source: Deep sequencing of the barcodes at different known bottleneck sizes (i.e., plated CFU) revealed that Nr and Nb both accurately quantified in vitro bottlenecks up to 105 CFU for this library, confirming the fidelity of these metrics and the absence of substantial technical artifacts during library preparation (e.g., PCR jackpots, contaminating barcodes; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: Mice were injected intravenously with 107 CFU of the barcoded ExPEC library.
source: Mice were injected intravenously with 107 CFU of the barcoded ExPEC library and were sacrificed beginning 4 hr post infection (hpi) and then daily up to 5 days post infection (dpi) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Describes experimental methods

claim: The blood, bile, left and right halves of the spleen, left and right kidney, left and right lung, and all four lobes of the liver were harvested at each time point.
source: The blood, bile, left and right halves of the spleen, left and right kidney, left and right lung, and all four lobes of the liver were harvested at each time point.
evidence: Describes experimental methods

claim: 4 mice each day were sacrificed from 0 to 4 days post infection, and 12 mice were sacrificed at 5 dpi, collectively yielding 384 CFU measurements across 12 suborgans and 6 time points.
source: 4 mice each day were sacrificed from 0 to 4 days post infection, and 12 mice were sacrificed at 5 dpi, collectively yielding 384 CFU measurements across 12 suborgans and 6 time points.
evidence: Describes experimental design

claim: Sequencing for STAMPR calculations was carried out on 322 samples that had nonzero CFU.
source: Sequencing for STAMPR calculations was carried out on 322 samples that had nonzero CFU.
evidence: Describes experimental methods

claim: The highest CFU values were found in blood and most organs 4 hpi (0 dpi).
source: As observed in previous studies (Smith et al., 2010), the highest CFU values were found in blood and most organs 4 hpi (0 dpi) and a few bacteria remained detectable in blood after 1 dpi (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and citation to Smith et al., 2010

claim: A few bacteria remained detectable in blood after 1 dpi.
source: As observed in previous studies (Smith et al., 2010), the highest CFU values were found in blood and most organs 4 hpi (0 dpi) and a few bacteria remained detectable in blood after 1 dpi (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The kidneys displayed a similar trend to blood, although some bacteria were detected up to 5 dpi in some animals.
source: The kidneys displayed a similar trend, although some bacteria were detected up to 5 dpi in some animals (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: The spleen contained more bacteria than the kidneys but still trended towards clearance.
source: The spleen contained more bacteria than the kidneys but still trended towards clearance (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: In the lung, even at 5 dpi, several hundred bacteria were present, suggesting that the lung has lower clearance capacities compared to the other organs.
source: In the lung, however, even at 5 dpi, several hundred bacteria were present, suggesting that the lung has lower clearance capacities compared to the other organs (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3, with inference about clearance capacity

claim: The rapid pathogen elimination from blood likely reflects clearance by filtrative organs like the liver and spleen, which had the highest bacterial burdens 4 hpi, rather than killing by blood.
source: The rapid pathogen elimination from blood likely reflects clearance by filtrative organs like the liver and spleen, which had the highest bacterial burdens 4 hpi, rather than killing by blood (e.g., complement), since mouse blood is permissive for E. coli growth (Marcus et al., 1954).
evidence: Inference based on data and citation to Marcus et al., 1954

claim: Mouse blood is permissive for E. coli growth.
source: The rapid pathogen elimination from blood likely reflects clearance by filtrative organs like the liver and spleen, which had the highest bacterial burdens 4 hpi, rather than killing by blood (e.g., complement), since mouse blood is permissive for E. coli growth (Marcus et al., 1954).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marcus et al., 1954

claim: Clearance failures were most prominent in the liver, which yielded the highest CFU values 5 dpi.
source: Clearance failures were most prominent in the liver, which yielded the highest CFU values 5 dpi (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: Hepatic bacterial burdens were bimodal, with some mice containing ~106 bacterial cells while littermates had ~104-fold fewer bacteria.
source: Hepatic bacterial burdens were bimodal, with some mice containing ~106 bacterial cells while littermates had ~104-fold fewer bacteria.
evidence: Describes data from the study

claim: Animals with high CFU had visible abscesses in the liver.
source: Notably, animals with high CFU had visible abscesses in the liver.
evidence: Describes observations from the study

claim: Lobes of the liver that lacked visible abscesses did not have high CFU, arguing against the presence of occult abscesses.
source: Lobes of the liver that lacked visible abscesses did not have high CFU, arguing against the presence of occult abscesses.
evidence: Describes observations and inference from the study

claim: High CFU were occasionally observed in additional organs outside the liver.
source: While CFU were usually cleared from organs outside the liver, high CFU were also occasionally observed in additional organs; for example, in one animal, the bacterial burden in the left and right lungs differed by 100-fold (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Three animals had very high bacterial burdens in the bile (~107 CFU/ml) aspirated from gallbladder samples from 4 and 5 dpi.
source: We also observed three animals with very high bacterial burdens in the bile (~107 CFU/ml) aspirated from gallbladder samples from 4 and 5 dpi (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: At 4 hpi, the number of blood CFU (~100) was nearly the same as the corresponding Nr (~80), indicating that at this point most bacteria possessed different tags.
source: At 4 hpi, when mice were still bacteremic, we observed that the number of blood CFU (~100) was nearly the same as the corresponding Nr (~80), indicating that at this point most bacteria possessed different tags, suggesting that there has been little replication in blood following inoculation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: At early time points both kidneys had Nr values similar to CFU, indicating minimal net replication.
source: Like the blood, at early time points both kidneys had Nr values similar to CFU, indicating minimal net replication (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: In the spleen at 4 hpi (0 dpi), Nr and Nb values were ~104, slightly less than CFU values.
source: In the spleen at 4 hpi (0 dpi), Nr and Nb values were ~104, slightly less than CFU values (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: By 5 dpi in the spleen, the CFU recovered (~20) was very close to values of Nr, indicating that these remaining cells had not undergone substantial replication.
source: By 5 dpi, the CFU recovered (~20) was very close to values of Nr, indicating that these remaining cells had not undergone substantial replication.
evidence: Describes data and inference from the study

claim: In the lungs, CFU approximated Nr, indicating that the bacterial population had undergone very little replication.
source: In the lungs, CFU approximated Nr, indicating that the bacterial population had undergone very little replication (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: The elevated hepatic CFU values were associated with clonal expansion events since Nr and Nb were orders of magnitude lower than CFU in animals with abscesses.
source: As discussed above, some of the largest bacterial burdens in these experiments were present in the liver at 5 dpi (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 4). The elevated hepatic CFU values were associated with clonal expansion events since Nr and Nb were orders of magnitude lower than CFU in animals with abscesses (Figure 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F, Figure 1J, and Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: At 1 dpi, two animals had clonal expansion (Nr/Nb >1000) in multiple liver lobes where ~ 1% of barcodes comprised a large majority of the reads.
source: Even at 1 dpi, two animals had clonal expansion (Nr/Nb >1000) in multiple lobes (Figure 2E and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 4) where ~ 1% of barcodes comprised a large majority of the reads (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2E, 2G, 2E-H, and Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: At 5 dpi all animals had similar Nr values, despite some having abscesses and the concomitant 10,000-fold increase in bacterial burden.
source: Nevertheless, at 5 dpi all animals had similar Nr values, despite some having abscesses and the concomitant 10,000-fold increase in bacterial burden (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: The immune and physical factors that govern bottlenecks appear to be highly consistent between animals.
source: Thus, the immune and physical factors that govern bottlenecks appear to be highly consistent between animals.
evidence: Inference based on the consistency of Nr values across animals

claim: The focal and stochastic expansion of a few clones within abscesses, rather than a general increase in bacterial survival, explains the wide variance in liver CFUs.
source: Instead, the focal and stochastic expansion of a few clones within abscesses, rather than a general increase in bacterial survival, explains the wide variance in liver CFUs.
evidence: Inference based on data showing consistent Nr but variable CFU

claim: Nr values were more consistent and lower than CFU across all organs particularly at 5 dpi.
source: In general, these analyses revealed that Nr values were more consistent and lower than CFU across all organs particularly at 5 dpi, revealing that most observations of very high bacterial burden are driven by very few bacterial clones (Figure 1—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 2–4

claim: Apart from the lung, FP sizes decreased during the 5 days of observation.
source: Apart from the lung, FP sizes decreased during the 5 days of observation.
evidence: Describes data from the study

claim: The host forces that restrict the bacterial population in this model act throughout the infection and are not limited to the initial establishment of the pathogen population.
source: Therefore, the host forces that restrict the bacterial population in this model act throughout the infection and are not limited to the initial establishment of the pathogen population.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that FP sizes decreased over time

claim: Each organ is associated with a specific and distinct probability of yielding clonal expansion, likely reflecting their underlying biological/compositional differences.
source: However, each organ is associated with a specific and distinct probability of yielding clonal expansion, likely reflecting their underlying biological/compositional differences.
evidence: Inference based on organ-specific patterns of clonal expansion

claim: Genetic distance (GD) is small when two samples are highly related and large when samples are not related.
source: This metric, known as genetic distance (GD), is small when two samples are highly related and large when samples are not related.
evidence: Defines the GD metric

claim: Low GD values (~0.1–0.2) require that the same barcodes be relatively abundant, not simply present, in both samples.
source: Low GD values (~0.1–0.2) require that the same barcodes be relatively abundant, not simply present, in both samples.
evidence: Explains interpretation of GD metric

claim: RD ('resilient' genetic distance) quantifies the number of barcodes that contribute to the similarity between two populations in a manner that takes into account all detected barcodes.
source: GD is also influenced by outliers, and so a different metric, called RD ('resilient' genetic distance), quantifies the number of barcodes that contribute to the similarity between two populations in a manner that takes into account all detected barcodes (Hullahalli et al., 2021; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hullahalli et al., 2021 and Figure 1A

claim: If both RD and GD are low, only a few barcodes contribute to the genetic similarity between samples.
source: For example, if both RD and GD are low, only a few barcodes contribute to the genetic similarity between samples.
evidence: Explains interpretation of RD and GD metrics

claim: If RD is high and GD is low, the samples are similar because they share many barcodes, which often occurs when samples closely resemble the inoculum through recent temporal separation.
source: In contrast, if RD is high and GD is low, the samples are similar because they share many barcodes, which often occurs when samples closely resemble the inoculum through recent temporal separation.
evidence: Explains interpretation of RD and GD metrics

claim: Fractional RD (FRD) is a directional metric that quantifies the extent to which shared barcodes are represented by all barcodes in the sample.
source: RD can be normalized to the number of barcodes in a sample, and this 'fractional' RD (FRD) is a directional metric that quantifies the extent to which shared barcodes are represented by all barcodes in the sample.
evidence: Defines the FRD metric

claim: At 4 hpi, all organs possess highly similar bacterial populations that share many barcodes.
source: At 4 hpi, all organs possess highly similar bacterial populations that share many barcodes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) as they have only recently been separated from the inoculum.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: After 4 hpi, GD between organs generally increases over time, suggesting that the populations are not substantially disseminating and mixing.
source: After this initial capture of bacteria, GD between organs generally increases over time, suggesting that the populations are not substantially disseminating and mixing, and that populations within organs are continually being antagonized by host defense processes, consistent with overall decreases in CFU.
evidence: Inference based on increasing GD over time

claim: In mice with expanded clones in the liver 1 dpi, the dominant barcodes were not detected in other organs or other lobes of the liver, indicating that these expanded clones were locally confined.
source: In mice with expanded clones in the liver 1 dpi (e.g., Figure 2D–H), the dominant barcodes were not detected in other organs or other lobes of the liver, indicating that these expanded clones were locally confined (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, asterisks).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D-H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: In animals with liver abscesses apparent 4 or 5 dpi, the bacterial populations in the lobe with the abscess were largely distinct from populations in other organs.
source: Similarly, in animals with liver abscesses apparent 4 or 5 dpi, the bacterial populations in the lobe with the abscess were largely distinct from populations in other organs (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 6

claim: Dissection and comparison of individual abscesses from the same animal revealed that these populations were distinct.
source: Dissection and comparison of individual abscesses from the same animal revealed that these populations were distinct (Figure 4), suggesting that abscesses do not originate from the same bacterial population and do not substantially exchange bacteria.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4

claim: Multiple clones, rather than one, comprise a single abscess.
source: Surprisingly, multiple clones, rather than one, comprise a single abscess.
evidence: Describes findings from the study

claim: Bacterial expansion events in organs other than the liver were associated with dissemination.
source: In contrast to the liver, bacterial expansion events in other organs were associated with dissemination.
evidence: Describes findings from the study

claim: The most significant spreading events were observed when ExPEC reached the bile.
source: The most significant spreading events were observed when ExPEC reached the bile (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 5 [mice 17, 20], Figure 3—figure supplement 6 [mouse 31]).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 5, and Figure 3—figure supplement 6

claim: Each of the three animals with CFU in bile harbored a single highly dominant clone (>99% of all reads) and these clones spread systemically to multiple organs.
source: Each of the three animals with CFU in bile harbored a single highly dominant clone (>99% of all reads) and these clones spread systemically to multiple organs; however, the precise organs to which the clone disseminated varied across mice, suggesting that spread of these clones is stochastic (Figure 3—figure supplements 5–6).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 5–6

claim: FRDorgan-bile was significantly greater than the FRDbile-organ, confirming that systemic organs possess relatively more abundant nontransferred populations than bile.
source: Furthermore, FRDorgan-bile was significantly greater than the FRDbile-organ, confirming that systemic organs possess relatively more abundant nontransferred populations than bile (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C

claim: FRD values across all organs with some relatedness (GD < 0.8) decreased significantly over time, indicating that relatedness at later time points was the result of relatively few barcodes.
source: More broadly, FRD values across all organs with some relatedness (GD < 0.8) decreased significantly over time, indicating that relatedness at later time points was the result of relatively few barcodes (Figure 3D, few barcodes relative to the total barcodes in a sample, not the entire library).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Early genetic relatedness is driven by recent temporal separation (i.e., many barcodes), while later genetic relatedness is typically driven by the dissemination of a few clones.
source: Taken together, these results reveal that early genetic relatedness is driven by recent temporal separation (i.e., many barcodes), while later genetic relatedness is typically driven by the dissemination of a few clones.
evidence: Inference based on FRD data over time

claim: Clearance failures and systemic dissemination are mostly attributable to ~0.0001% of the inoculum.
source: Collectively, our data reveal that clearance failures and systemic dissemination are mostly attributable to ~0.0001% of the inoculum.
evidence: Inference based on data showing clonal expansion from very few cells

claim: The manifestation of clonal expansion and dissemination events is highly variable across mice but can fall into three trajectories: (1) complete clearance without dissemination, (2) clonal expansion without dissemination (e.g., liver abscesses), and (3) clonal expansion with dissemination (e.g., bile).
source: The manifestation of these events is highly variable across mice but can fall into three trajectories: (1) complete clearance without dissemination, (2) clonal expansion without dissemination (e.g., liver abscesses), and (3) clonal expansion with dissemination (e.g., bile).
evidence: Summarizes findings from the study

claim: A fourfold increase in dose resulted in ExPEC burdens in the spleen ~2.5-fold greater than in the low-dose group.
source: Splenic CFU was highly consistent within groups, as observed above, and a fourfold increase in dose resulted in ExPEC burdens ~2.5-fold greater than in the low-dose group (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Nb and Nr in the spleen were significantly larger in the high-dose group, suggesting that there is a general correlation between dose, CFU burdens, and FP sizes in the spleen.
source: Nb and Nr in the spleen were also relatively similar within the groups, indicating relatively uniform barcode distributions, and both values were significantly larger in the high-dose group, suggesting that there is a general correlation between dose, CFU burdens, and FP sizes in the spleen.
evidence: Describes data and inference from the study

claim: There was a reduction in the bacterial burden in the liver at the high dose due to a greater incidence of abscesses in the low-dose group (6/10 animals) compared to the high-dose group (2/9 animals).
source: Unexpectedly, there was a reduction in the bacterial burden in the liver at the high dose; a greater incidence of abscesses in the low-dose group (6/10 animals) compared to the high-dose group (2/9 animals) led to a reduction in median CFU at the high dose.
evidence: Describes data from the study

claim: Despite the higher hepatic burdens in animals given the low dose, Nr was significantly higher in animals given the high dose, reflecting the role of clonal expansion in elevated CFU.
source: Despite the higher hepatic burdens in animals given the low dose, Nr was significantly higher in animals given the high dose, reflecting the role of clonal expansion in elevated CFU.
evidence: Describes data and inference from the study

claim: The scaling of FP with dose reveals that a fixed fraction, not number, of bacterial cells from the inoculum survive clearance mechanisms up to 5 dpi.
source: The scaling of FP with dose reveals that a fixed fraction, not number, of bacterial cells from the inoculum survive clearance mechanisms up to 5 dpi.
evidence: Inference based on the relationship between dose and FP

claim: In the liver, the dramatic replication of very few clones obscures the relationship between dose and CFU.
source: However, in contrast to the spleen, the dramatic replication of very few clones in the liver obscures this relationship from being detected by CFU alone.
evidence: Inference based on data showing high CFU but low Nr in some animals

claim: There was an increase in splenic CFU 5 dpi in animals treated with clodronate.
source: There was an increase in splenic CFU 5 dpi in animals treated with clodronate, whereas this difference was more subtle in the liver, lungs, and kidneys (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Macrophage depletion increased FP sizes in the liver, spleen, and kidneys.
source: Nb and Nr calculations revealed that macrophage depletion increased FP sizes in the liver, spleen, and kidneys, although the difference in the lung was not statistically significant.
evidence: Describes data from the study

claim: The significant increase in FP, but not CFU, after clodronate treatment in the liver is explained by two animals in the control group with the dramatic expansion of very few clones.
source: The significant increase in FP, but not CFU, after clodronate treatment in the liver is explained by two animals in the control group with the dramatic expansion of very few clones (Figure 5B, red and black circles).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Macrophage depletion widens the bottlenecks in the liver, spleen, and kidney.
source: Since clodronate treatment increased both FP and CFU, macrophage depletion widens the bottlenecks in the liver, spleen, and kidney.
evidence: Inference based on data showing increased FP and CFU after clodronate treatment

claim: Increased dose and macrophage depletion widened bottlenecks in the host but did not increase the levels of bacterial replication.
source: In this model, increased dose and macrophage depletion widened bottlenecks in the host but did not increase the levels of bacterial replication.
evidence: Inference based on data from dose and clodronate experiments

claim: There was a predominance of cell envelope homeostasis genes and gene clusters that were underrepresented in liver samples, including mlaFEDCB, ftsEX, envZ/ompR, and many LPS biosynthetic genes.
source: There was a predominance of cell envelope homeostasis genes and gene clusters that were underrepresented in liver samples, including mlaFEDCB (Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009; Ekiert et al., 2017), ftsEX (Du et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2011), envZ/ompR (Hall and Silhavy, 1981), and many LPS biosynthetic genes (Figure 6A), suggesting that cell envelope homeostasis across multiple pathways is required for extraintestinal survival.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6A and citations

claim: Another coherent set of underrepresented genes in the liver included manA, nagAB, and pgi, which convert mannose-6-phosphate, n-acetylglucosamine-6-phosphate (GlcNAc-6P), and glucose-6-phosphate into fructose-6-phophate, respectively.
source: Another coherent set of underrepresented genes in the liver included manA, nagAB, and pgi, which convert mannose-6-phosphate, n-acetylglucosamine-6-phosphate (GlcNAc-6P), and glucose-6-phosphate into fructose-6-phophate, respectively (Paixão et al., 2015; Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6B and citation to Paixão et al., 2015

claim: nagK was not underrepresented in the liver, suggesting that the host is the source of GlcNAc.
source: Interestingly, nagK was not underrepresented in the liver, suggesting that the host is the source of GlcNAc.
evidence: Inference based on the absence of nagK from underrepresented genes

claim: Several cell envelope homeostasis pathways are important for early survival in the liver and an additional requirement for fructose-6-phosphate during systemic infection.
source: Taken together, the screen revealed that several cell envelope homeostasis pathways are important for early survival in the liver and an additional requirement for fructose-6-phosphate during systemic infection.
evidence: Summarizes findings from the transposon screen

claim: In the liver, all genes found to be underrepresented in the transposon screen displayed fitness defects.
source: In the liver, all genes found to be underrepresented in the transposon screen displayed fitness defects.
evidence: Describes findings from the barcoded mutant validation

claim: The magnitude of the defects in the mlaC, ftsX, yejM, and nagA mutants were far more pronounced than that observed in the manA mutant, which possessed modest but consistent defects relative to the WT.
source: However, the magnitude of the defects in the mlaC, ftsX, yejM, and nagA mutants were far more pronounced than that observed in the manA mutant, which possessed modest but consistent defects relative to the WT.

claim: There was no difference between ∆manA and ∆nagA compared to ∆nagK and WT in the lungs, indicating that these genes have organ-specific importance for ExPEC survival.
source: Intriguingly, there was no difference between ∆manA and ∆nagA compared to ∆nagK and WT in the lungs, indicating that these genes have organ-specific importance for ExPEC survival and reveals that the lung microenvironment has particularly distinct selective effects (Figure 7C).

claim: The ∆nagK negative control was identical to the WT across all organs 1 dpi.
source: The ∆nagK negative control was identical to the WT across all organs 1 dpi.
evidence: Describes findings from the barcoded mutant validation

claim: The differential importance of nagA and nagK confirms the TIS results and provides further evidence that the source of GlcNAc-6P is the host.
source: The differential importance of nagA and nagK confirms our transposon insertion sequencing (TIS) results and provides further evidence that the source of GlcNAc-6P is the host.

claim: The ∆mlaC, ∆ftsX, and ∆yejM strains were significantly depleted in the spleen, liver (with or without abscesses), and lungs relative to the WT at 5 dpi.
source: The ∆mlaC, ∆ftsX, and ∆yejM strains were significantly depleted in the spleen, liver (with or without abscesses), and lungs relative to the WT at 5 dpi, further highlighting the essentiality of the cell envelope-related process to survival within these organs (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7B-D

claim: Despite having clear defects at 1 dpi, ∆nagA and ∆manA were indistinguishable from WT and ∆nagK in the spleen and the liver at 5 dpi, regardless of the presence of abscesses.
source: In contrast, despite having clear defects at 1 dpi, ∆nagA and ∆manA were indistinguishable from WT and ∆nagK in the spleen and the liver at 5 dpi, regardless of the presence of abscesses.
evidence: Describes findings from the barcoded mutant validation

claim: ∆nagA was significantly more abundant in the lungs than the WT or ∆nagK at 5 dpi.
source: To our surprise, ∆nagA was significantly more abundant in the lungs than the WT or ∆nagK at 5 dpi (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Cell envelope and sugar metabolism genes likely contribute to distinct mechanisms that facilitate ExPEC survival, in the face of host factors that fluctuate over time and between organs.
source: Therefore, cell envelope and sugar metabolism genes likely contribute to distinct mechanisms that facilitate ExPEC survival, in the face of host factors that fluctuate over time and between organs.
evidence: Inference based on the differential fitness of mutants over time and across organs

claim: The pathogen factors that are required for the initial establishment of infection differ from those required to survive later or clonally expand.
source: These results further reveal that the pathogen factors that are required for the initial establishment of infection differ from those required to survive later or clonally expand.
evidence: Inference based on the differential fitness of mutants at 1 dpi vs 5 dpi

claim: ExPEC requires hexose metabolism to establish populations within specific organs, but this pathway is not required by the subpopulations that ultimately persist later in the infection or clonally expand.
source: Specifically, ExPEC requires hexose metabolism to establish populations within specific organs, but this pathway is not required by the subpopulations that ultimately persist later in the infection or clonally expand, suggesting that establishment, persistence, and expansion depend on distinct pathogen pathways.
evidence: Inference based on the differential fitness of hexose metabolism mutants at 1 dpi vs 5 dpi

claim: Most organs continuously restricted the pathogen population over time, indicated by decreasing Nr values over time.
source: In general, most organs continuously restricted the pathogen population over time, indicated by decreasing Nr values over time.
evidence: Describes findings from the study

claim: A notable exception to the trend of decreasing Nr over time was the lungs, where FP values largely plateaued by 2 dpi.
source: A notable exception to this trend was the lungs, where FP values largely plateaued by 2 dpi, explaining why this organ had among the highest FP sizes 5 dpi.
evidence: Describes findings from the study

claim: Clodronate had no effect on CFU in the lung.
source: In addition, clodronate had no effect on CFU in the lung and some mutants defective for survival in the liver were more abundant than WT in the lung.
evidence: Describes findings from the study

claim: The lung microenvironment is less hostile to ExPEC, perhaps reflecting distinct cellular niches occupied by ExPEC in the lungs relative to the liver or spleen.
source: These three lines of evidence indicate that the lung microenvironment is less hostile to ExPEC, perhaps reflecting distinct cellular niches (e.g., different immune cell compositions and nutrient availabilities) occupied by ExPEC in the lungs relative to the liver or spleen.
evidence: Inference based on multiple lines of evidence from the study

claim: The liver and lungs differ markedly in their clearance defects; the liver appears more permissive for ExPEC replication, whereas the lung appears more permissive for bacterial survival.
source: Thus, the liver and lungs appear to differ markedly in their clearance defects; the liver appears more permissive for ExPEC replication, whereas the lung appears more permissive for bacterial survival.
evidence: Inference based on findings from the study

claim: E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae are among the leading causes of liver abscesses in humans.
source: E. coli, and more recently Klebsiella pneumoniae, are among the leading causes of liver abscesses in humans, and patients with liver abscesses with associated bacteremia are at higher risk for mortality (Meddings et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meddings et al., 2010

claim: Patients with liver abscesses with associated bacteremia are at higher risk for mortality.
source: E. coli, and more recently Klebsiella pneumoniae, are among the leading causes of liver abscesses in humans, and patients with liver abscesses with associated bacteremia are at higher risk for mortality (Meddings et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meddings et al., 2010

claim: Mice are substantially more resistant to LPS than humans.
source: Furthermore, the i.v. doses used here do not directly model doses likely encountered by humans; however, mice are substantially more resistant to LPS than humans, and higher doses in mice may mimic the lower doses humans are likely to encounter (Copeland et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Copeland et al., 2005

claim: In S. aureus dissemination, bottlenecks widened in size with infectious dose and macrophage depletion.
source: In one study, i.v. inoculation of a S. aureus pool consisting of three differentially marked strains revealed several trends observed here (Pollitt et al., 2018). Although the use of three markers limited the resolution, this study of S. aureus dissemination also found that bottlenecks (measured as the proportion of organs with less than two strains) widened in size with infectious dose and macrophage depletion.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pollitt et al., 2018

claim: Unlike ExPEC where expansion of clones in liver abscesses remained locally confined, S. aureus dissemination from the liver was thought to result in clonal abscesses in the kidney.
source: However, unlike ExPEC where expansion of clones in liver abscesses remained locally confined, S. aureus dissemination from the liver was thought to result in clonal abscesses in the kidney.
evidence: Compares findings from this study with S. aureus studies

claim: Abscess formation is much more consistently observed for S. aureus than for ExPEC.
source: In general, abscess formation is much more consistently observed for S. aureus (Sx et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2009), whereas this outcome is apparently stochastic in this ExPEC model.
evidence: Supported by citations to Sx et al., 2014 and Cheng et al., 2009

claim: In P. aeruginosa, the pathogen consistently replicated in the bile and these cells became the source of bacteria in the intestinal tract.
source: Another study examining systemic P. aeruginosa population dynamics with STAMP found that the pathogen consistently replicated in the bile and these cells became the source of bacteria in the intestinal tract (Bachta et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bachta et al., 2020

claim: The FP of the bile population in ExPEC was ~1, whereas the P. aeruginosa FP was ~10 times greater.
source: The FP of the bile population in our study was ~1, whereas we calculated that the P. aeruginosa FP was ~10 times greater (Hullahalli et al., 2021).
evidence: Compares findings from this study with P. aeruginosa studies, supported by citation to Hullahalli et al., 2021

claim: The more restrictive bottleneck for ExPEC potentially explains why transit to the bile is stochastic with this pathogen.
source: The more restrictive bottleneck for ExPEC potentially explains why transit to the bile is stochastic with this pathogen.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of FP values between ExPEC and P. aeruginosa

claim: In models of overwhelming bacteremia, genetic determinants often encode surface structures, such as the capsule in K1 ExPEC.
source: In models of overwhelming bacteremia, these genetic determinants often encode surface structures, such as the capsule in K1 ExPEC (McCarthy et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to McCarthy et al., 2018

claim: There was little overlap between genes identified as underrepresented in the liver or spleen in this study and genes identified in a previous study using a similar experimental system.
source: Unexpectedly, there was little overlap between genes we identified to be underrepresented in the liver or spleen and genes identified as underrepresented in a previous study using a similar experimental system (Subashchandrabose et al., 2013).
evidence: Compares findings from this study with previous study, supported by citation to Subashchandrabose et al., 2013

claim: Different strains of mice impose distinct barriers to infection, altering the pathogen genetic requirements for infection.
source: A potential explanation for this discrepancy is that Subashchandrabose et al. performed their experiments in a different mouse background (CBA/J), and different strains of mice impose distinct barriers to infection, altering the pathogen genetic requirements for infection (Cunrath and Bumann, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cunrath and Bumann, 2019

claim: Early stochastic clonal expansion events were detected in every experiment in this study using three independent libraries and distinct approaches.
source: Early stochastic clonal expansion events were detected in every experiment in our study using three independent libraries and distinct approaches (STAMPR, transposon libraries, and barcoded mutants).
evidence: Describes findings from the study

claim: Clonal expansion events underlie variation in infection outcomes.
source: These expansion events underlie variation in infection outcomes.
evidence: Inference based on findings from the study

claim: Clonal expansion events appear to fall into two functional categories – those that are due to dissemination (e.g., from bile) and those that are not (e.g., liver abscesses).
source: While dissection of the mechanism(s) that account for this stochasticity is beyond the scope of this study, our observations suggest that several factors account for and modulate clonal expansion. Such events appear to fall into two functional categories – those that are due to dissemination (e.g., from bile) and those that are not (e.g., liver abscesses).
evidence: Inference based on findings from the study

claim: There is an apparent inverse correlation between infectious dose and liver abscess formation.
source: In the latter, we observed an apparent inverse correlation with infectious dose, although more animals are required to reach statistical significance (Figure 5A).
evidence: Describes observation from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 5A

claim: More robust early immune induction (presumably elicited with a higher dose) disproportionately clears bacteria.
source: This trend suggests that more robust early immune induction (presumably elicited with a higher dose) disproportionately clears bacteria, a hypothesis that has also been generated by mathematical modeling (Ellner et al., 2021; Duneau et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on data, supported by citations to Ellner et al., 2021 and Duneau et al., 2017

claim: There are apparent lobe (more frequent in the right lobe) and topological (all on the surface) biases in liver abscess formation.
source: Additionally, we observed apparent lobe (more frequent in the right lobe) and topological (all on the surface) biases in liver abscess formation, raising the possibility that anatomic differences between lobes and their relative locations contribute to apparently stochastic outcomes as some lobes may be more likely to be seeded (due to blood flow) and more permissive to bacterial replication.
evidence: Describes observations from the study

claim: Clonal expansion explains why bacterial burden is highly variable in ExPEC and may also explain high variability in systemic infection outcomes in other bacteria.
source: Furthermore, clonal expansion explains why bacterial burden is highly variable in ExPEC and may also explain high variability in systemic infection outcomes in other bacteria (Crépin et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference based on findings from the study, supported by citation to Crépin et al., 2018

claim: Causative genotypic changes are unlikely to be linked to pathogen clonal expansion in liver abscesses.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that causative genotypic changes are unlikely to be linked to pathogen clonal expansion in liver abscesses, but we cannot definitively exclude this possibility.
evidence: Inference based on multiple lines of evidence from the study

claim: Expanded clones in the liver arise as early as 1 dpi, which is relatively early in the infection processes when relatively little bacterial replication has occurred.
source: Expanded clones in the liver arise as early as 1 dpi, which is relatively early in the infection processes when relatively little bacterial replication has occurred.
evidence: Describes findings from the study

claim: Different sets of barcodes expanded across all three experimental barcoded libraries.
source: If causative mutants existed in the inoculum prior to infection (e.g., in the colony that was picked to generate the barcoded strain), we would expect the same set of barcodes to expand; however, different sets of barcodes expanded across all three experimental barcoded libraries (e.g., abscess clones in Figure 4 are different).
evidence: Describes findings from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4

claim: Liver abscesses are relatively small and discrete but consist of multiple clones.
source: Furthermore, since liver abscesses are relatively small and discrete but consist of multiple clones, causative mutations would have had to arise in different bacterial cells that were also clustered together in physical space, which seems extremely unlikely.
evidence: Describes findings from the study

claim: Beneficial mutations would accumulate if bacteria isolated from abscesses were used to inoculate another set of mice and the process repeated for several passages.
source: Notably, despite tight bottlenecks, we predict that beneficial mutations would accumulate if bacteria isolated from abscesses were used to inoculate another set of mice and the process repeated for several passages, as has been observed with S. aureus passages in sheep over hundreds of days (Bacigalupe et al., 2019).
evidence: Prediction based on findings from the study, supported by citation to Bacigalupe et al., 2019
